div.p: Real-time embedded systems are becoming more complex to include multiple functionalities. Sharing a computing platform is a natural and effective solution to reducing the cost of those systems. However, the sharing can cause serious problems in mixed-criticality systems where applications have different levels of criticality. Certifying the mixed-criticality systems requires efficient scheduling algorithms and schedulability tests different from the ones used in single criticality systems.

In this paper, we propose the first dynamic scheduling algorithm called CBEDF for certifiable mixed-criticality systems on a uniprocessor platform. We show that CBEDF dominates previously proposed algorithms OCBP. In addition, we propose a sufficient schedulability test for CBEDF. We demonstrate that the schedulability test of CBEDF outperforms that of the previously proposed algorithms by performing simulations using randomly generated instances of jobs.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Modern real-time embedded systems are pressured to reduce their costs and physical resources such as size and energy consumption. [7] Implementing multiple functionalities into a shared computing platform is a natural and effective solution. However, the sharing can cause serious problems where applications have different levels of criticality.

Suppose ABS (high-critical system) and infortainment system (low-critical system) for vehicles share computing resources. The jobs for the infortainment system can cause deadline misses of the jobs for the ABS system by occupying the shared computing resources longer than expected. This situation can cause incorrect controls of the vehicles, which could result in severe safety problems such as car accidents.
To avoid these safety problems, we need new methodologies to handle these mixed-criticality systems.

According to [1], "Mixed-criticality is the concept of allowing applications at different levels of criticality to interact and co-exist on the same computational platform". The work in [1] introduces four major challenges of the mixed-criticality systems. One of the challenges is certification by design whose purpose is identifying and assessing "certifiability" of a component by formal and analytical methods. Recently, the certification issues for the mixedcriticality systems are researched by real-time groups. Their work mainly deals with scheduling and schedulabiilty analysis for the mixed-criticality systems [5,11,10]. However, the proposed scheduling algorithms for the certification of the mixed-criticality systems are based on fixed-priority scheduling. So, the algorithms cannot use computing resources efficiently because the algorithm does not care about runtime situations such as early finishes of jobs.

In this paper, we propose a dynamic scheduling algorithm for the certification of dual-criticality systems on a uniprocessor environment. The proposed algorithm is based on traditional Earliest Deadline First (EDF) algorithm [12] and criticality of each job. So, we call this new algorithm Criticality Based Earliest Deadline First (CBEDF). We show that CBEDF scheduling algorithm dominates previously proposed Own Criticality Based Priority (OCBP) scheduling algorithm [5]. Also, we propose a load-based sufficient schedulability test for CBEDF. We show that the schedulability test of CBEDF outperforms that of OCBP [11] and that of EDF [11] by experimenting with randomly generated instance sets.

This paper is organized as follows: In Section 2, we review related work. In Section 3, we present a formal model for dual-criticality real-time system and important terminologies used throughout this paper. Our new scheduling algorithm (CBEDF) for certifiable dual-criticality systems is proposed and proved that it dominates OCBP in Section 4. Then, we propose a sufficient schedulabilty test for CBEDF in Section 5. In Section 6, we show that schedulability of CBEDF outperforms those of the previously proposed algorithms by showing experimental results. Finally, we conclude this paper in Section 7.

div.head: RELATED WORK
div.p: Recently, many papers related to the mixed-criticality systems are published. Vestal [16] introduced the scheduling problem of multiple criticality system first by identifying and formalizing the problem. He first assumes that a task may have multiple worst-case execution times, each of which assures a different level of confidence. Then, he proposed two ideas which improve schedulability of multi-criticality systems. One is period transformation and the other is applying Audsley's priority assignment algorithm [2].

F. Dorin et al. [8] researched on schedulability and sensitivity of multiple criticality systems. They proved that the Audsley's algorithm is optimal for scheduling multiple criticality independent task systems with constrained-deadlines under a fixed-task-priority policy. S. Baruah et al. [6] studied on feasibility and schedulability of multiple-criticality systems and do the feasibility and schedulability analysis of EDF and fixed-priority scheduling algorithms for multicriticality real-time systems on preemptive uniprocessor platform.

Certification of mixed-criticality systems has been recently studied. S. Baruah et al. [5] showed that reservationbased scheduling approach is pessimistic in terms of utilization of resources for the mixed-criticality systems. To improve utilization, they propose an effective scheduling algorithm (OCBP) which is a priority-based scheduling algorithm for the mixed-criticality systems. They showed the effectiveness of the algorithm on dual-criticality systems by finding upper bound of speedup factor for each algorithm. After that, they extend their work to multi-criticality systems by deriving a quantitative processor speedup factor [4].

H. Li et al. [11] proposed load-based schedulability analysis for OCBP scheduling algorithm. Their schedulabilty analysis shows that OCBP scheduling algorithm outperforms the prior algorithms that have been used to schedule certifiable mixed-criticality systems. They extend the OCBP algorithm to certifiable mixed-criticality sporadic task systems [10].

The main target of our research is certifiable mixedcriticality systems like above papers [5,11,10]. Because the prior algorithms are based on a fixed-priority policy, the algorithm cannot consider runtime situations. On the other hand, our algorithm is based on a dynamic-priority policy. Thus, our algorithm outperforms prior works by considering runtime situations better as will be shown later.

There are some papers dealing with other issues on mixedcriticality systems. D. de Niz et al. [7] solved criticality inversion problem on mixed-criticality task sets on a uniprocessor platform by presenting a new scheduling scheme with asymmetric protection. It only prevents interference to highercritical tasks from lower-critical tasks. The proposed scheduling algorithm consists of two parts, offline and online. The offline algorithm identifies zero-slack instant for each task. The discovered zero-slack instant is used by a priority-based scheduler at runtime. They also proposed two metrics to evaluate the proposed scheduling algorithm. First is mixedcriticality blocking which measures how much blocking reduction is possible in specific task sets. Second is laxity utilization which measures how well a scheduling algorithm reduces the mixed-criticality blocking of the task set to make the task set schedulable.

K. Lakshmanan et al. [9] captured mixed-criticality property on distributed mixed-criticality cyber-physical systems by developing a formal metric called ductility which characterizes overload behavior of the systems. Also, they proposed a ductility-maximization packing algorithm, known as Compress-On-Packing (COP), which extends the asymmetric scheme of Zero-Slack Rate Monotonic (ZSRM) for distributed systems.

M. S. Mollison et al. [14] proposed a layered architecture for mixed-criticality scheduling problem on multicore platforms. Tasks at each criticality level are scheduled on different layers which have different intra-container schedulers. Lower layer for lower criticality tasks uses slacks generated by upper layer for higher criticality tasks. R. Pellizzoni et al. [15] introduced an innovative design methodology and architectural platform which ensures strong isolation guarantees to applications with different criticalities by using a reservation-based approach.

div.head: DUAL-CRITICALITY JOB MODEL AND TERMINOLOGY
div.p: In this section, we formally define a dual-criticality job model and introduce important terminologies used throughout this paper. We consider scheduling of dual-criticality systems on a preemptive uniprocessor platform. Although multiple criticality recurrent task system is interesting, many issues on the dual-criticality and uniprocessor system remain unsolved yet. Thus, we need to solve these simple cases first. Results from these simple cases will be used to solve more complex problems such as recurrent task system, multiple criticality systems and multiprocessor systems Before defining the dual-criticality job model, readers need to understand the certification of mixed-criticality systems.

There are several Certification Authorities (CA) for automotive systems to evaluate safetiness of vehicles in the world. Main interests of the CAs are certifying safety of the automotive systems. Thus, CAs do not care about jobs which are not directly related to safety like the navigation system. Instead, they evaluate correctness of only safety-critical jobs rigorously. On the other hand, the system developers try to certify correctness of the system functionalities. Thus, they should care about non-safety-critical jobs as well as safetycritical jobs. The certification process is less rigorous than CA's certification process. We can characterize this differnce certification between CA and developers using different methods to estimate Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET).

• Non-safety-critical certification: To estimate WCET, system developers analyze both low(non-safety) and high(safety) critical jobs with simple methods (ex: experiments). With the measured WCET, the system developers try to certify the low and high critical jobs are correctly operateed within their deadlines.

div.head: • Safety-critical certification:
div.p: To estimate WCET, CAs analyze the high critical jobs with complex methods (ex: worst case path analysis [17]). As a result, WCET measured by CAs have more time-margins than WCET measured by system developers. With the WCET measured by CAs, CAs try to certify that the high critical jobs are correctly operated within their deadlines.

div.head: Dual-Criticality Job Model
div.p: A dual-criticality instance I = {J1, ..., Jn} is composed of n dual-criticality jobs, where each job Ji is characterized by a 5-tuple of parameters: Ji = {Ai, Di, χi, Ci, ESi}. Our job model is based on that in [11] and adds another parameter.
• Ai : Release time of Ji.
• Di : Deadline of Ji. We assume that Di ≥ Ai

div.head: Definition of Important Terminologies
div.p: Definitions of the terminologies used in this paper are based on those in [5,11]. We briefly define the terminologies to understand the rest of this paper easily. (refer to [5,11] to see the more detailed explanations) Behavior (γ1, ..., γn) : Each job Ji executes for some amount of time, γi, at runtime. The γi units of time should be executed on its scheduling window [Ai, Di] to meet its deadline. A behavior of an instance is a collection of γi for all the jobs Ji in the instance.

div.head: Criticality Level L(I):
div.p: The criticality level of a behavior (γ1, ..., γn) of an instance I is defined to be LO if γi ≤ Ci(LO) for all i, and HI if γi > Ci(LO) for any i. If any γi > Ci(HI), then we define the behavior is erroneous. In other words, if at least one job uses more than Ci(LO) units of time for its execution, the criticality level of the behaviors becomes HI.

div.head: Correctness of mixed-criticality scheduling:
div.p: A scheduling algorithm is correct dual-criticality scheduling algorithm if the algorithm satisfies the following two conditions:
correct scheduling algorithm can allocate sufficient execution times to every job between its release time and deadline.

• If L(I) = HI, correct scheduling algorithm can allocate sufficient execution times to all high critical jobs between their releases times and deadlines. Meeting deadlines of low critical jobs do not need to be considered.

Load: Load [13] means the maximum usage rate over all the time intervals. LO-criticality load, LoadLO(I), and HIcriticality load, LoadHI(I), of a dual-criticality instance I are defined by the following two formulas: Load LO (I) = max
div.formula: 0≤t 1 <t 2 J i :t 1 ≤A i ∧D i <t 2 C i (LO) t 2 -t 1
div.p: Load HI (I) = max
div.formula: 0≤t 1 <t 2 J i :χ i =HI∧t 1 ≤A i ∧D i <t 2 C i (HI) t 2 -t 1
div.p: ,where t1 is a release time of a job and t2 is a deadline of a job. Thus, we need n 2 time to calculate the two loads to consider all the time intervals [t1,t2].

div.head: OUR PROPOSED DYNAMIC SCHEDUL-ING ALGORITHM : CBEDF
div.p: In this section, we propose a new scheduling algorithm for certifiable dual-criticality systems. We call this algorithm Criticality Based Earliest Deadline First (CBEDF) since CBEDF is based on the traditional Earliest Deadline First (EDF) scheduling algorithm [12]. CBEDF apply EDF scheduling algorithm to schedule jobs which have same criticality. It means that jobs having same criticality are scheduled in EDF order. We will explain how to schedule jobs which have different criticalities.

div.head: Basic Idea
div.p: Suppose all HI critical jobs are guaranteed to reserve their Ci(HI) units of time on their scheduling window. Then, LO critical jobs can use the following two kinds of free slacks.

div.head: • Remaining Slack: At runtime, a high critical job
div.p: Ji finishes eariler than its deadline. Then, the time interval between Ci(LO) and Ci(HI) is available for other jobs. We call this interval remaining slack as shown in Figure 1(Upper).

• Empty Slack: If there are available units of time when all HI critical jobs are reserved their Ci(HI) units of time, then we call the available units of time empty slack. Figure 1(Lower) shows the empty slack concept.
The basic idea of our algorithm is allocating the two kinds of free slacks to LO critical jobs to improve utilization.

Relative locations of remaining slacks cannot be changed in order to improve utilization because they rely on locations of HI critical jobs. In contrast, locations of empty slacks can be changed to improve utilization. We will explain how to find the suitable locations for empty slacks.

div.head: Off-line Empty Slack Location Discovery
div.p: Suppose all HI critical jobs are guaranteed to reserve their Ci(HI) units of time by scheduling the HI critical jobs first. Then empty slacks are formed between these reserved units of time. However, these locations of the empty slacks are not suitable to achieve high utilization. We illustrate this with an example below.

Example 1 Consider an instance I comprised of three jobs. The jobs are characterized as below. In this example, we characterize the jobs with a 4-tuple (Ai, Di, χi, Ci) model proposed in [5], because the algorithm for discovering empty slack location is not explained yet. J1 = (0, 2, HI, {1, 1}) J2 = (2, 3, LO, {1, 1}) J3 = (0, 5, HI, {2, 2})

If J1 and J3 are scheduled first using criticality-based scheduling algorithm, then J2 misses its deadline because there is no remaining slack and no empty slack before its deadline as shown in Figure 2(Upper). However, if the empty slacks are located as shown in Figure 2(Lower), all the three jobs can be scheduled without any deadline miss because J2 can be scheduled in interval [2,3]. Consequently, we need to identify suitable locations for empty slacks to improve utilization.

Fortunately, we can identify suitable locations for empty slacks by locating HI critical jobs as close to their deadlines as possible. If all HI critical jobs are scheduled in EDF order and each HI critical job is located as close to its deadline as possible, then the HI critical jobs have empty slacks before their reserved slacks as shown in Figure 2(Lower).

Suppose IHI = {Ji | χi = HI} and IHI is sorted in ascending order according to job's deadlines. Hence, IHI = {JH1, ..., JHn} where DH1 ≤ ...... ≤ DHn. Then, a HI critical job has DHi -AHi -CHi(HI) units of time for its empty slack. The empty slack can be used by other HI critical jobs as shown in Figure 3. Thus, the empty slack size is decreased by the other HI critical jobs. Consequently, calculating empty slack size should consider the decreased size. We can calculate the empty slack size for each HI critical job with following equations.
div.formula: ESHi = ⎧ ⎪ ⎪ ⎨ ⎪ ⎪ ⎩ (DHi -DHi-1) -ISHi -CHi(HI) , if (DHi -DHi-1) -ISHi -Ci(HI) > 0 0 , otherwise ISHi = ⎧ ⎪ ⎪ ⎪ ⎪ ⎪ ⎨ ⎪ ⎪ ⎪ ⎪ ⎪ ⎩ (DHi -DHi+1) + ISHi+1 + CHi+1(HI) , if (DHi -DHi+1) + ISHi+1 + CHi+1(HI) > 0 0 , if i = n 0 , otherwise
div.p: ESHi is the empty slack size of a HI critical job JHi. ISHi is the units of time used by other HI critical jobs for JHi. As shown in the above equations, AHi is replaced with DHi-1 when calculating ESHi because JHi-1 should be located as close to its deadline as possible. Hence, the empty slack of JHi can exist after DHi-1.
Because each HI critical job has information about empty slack allocated to it, the empty slack size of all the HI critical jobs should be determined before their execution.
Our empty slack discovering algorithm scans all the HI critical jobs from JHn to JHi to calculate the empty slack size for the HI critical jobs. Thus, time complexity of the algorithm is O(n)

div.head: Scheduling at Runtime
div.p: In this section, we will explain how to apply our new scheduling algorithm at runtime. As we explained before, CBEDF applies traditional EDF scheduling algorithm to jobs having same criticality. Thus, we need two run-queues (one for HI critical jobs, the other for LO critical jobs) because we assume dual-criticality systems. As shown in Figure 4, CBEDF scheduling algorithm schedules a given instance for four cases as follows:

1. There is no ready job. 2. There are only LO critical ready jobs. For cases 1, 2 and 3, CBEDF scheduling algorithm dispatches any ready jobs because considering criticality of jobs is meaningless for the cases. For case 4, CBEDF scheduling algorithm checks whether current slack is a free slack or not. If so (remaining or empty slack), then a LO critical job is dispatched to the current slack. Otherwise, a HI critical job is dispatched. Runtime scheduling process is described in detail with Example 2 and Figure 5. At time 0, there are both LO and HI critical ready jobs (J1, J2, J4). So, we need to check whether current slack is a free slack or not. In this situation, current slack is not a free slack. Thus, the job at the head of the HI-queue is dispatched as shown in the first figure of Figure 5.

At time 1, there are two possible cases. The first case is that the dispatched job J1 is not finished by its C1(LO) units of time. So, L(I) becomes HI. Thus, all the HI critical jobs should be guaranteed to reserve their Ci(HI) units of time. Continuously, J1 is finished at time 2 and J4 is dispatched to the empty slack for J2. After that, J2 is dispatched to interval [3,5] as shown in the second figure of Figure 5. In first case, J3 misses its deadline. However, it does not matter because L(I) is HI.

Second case is that the dispatched job J1 is finished by its C1(LO) units of time. So, a remaining slack is formed As shown above, any behaviors of the instance used in Example 2 can be scheduled by CBEDF without any deadline miss. We say that the instance in Example 2 is CBEDFschedulable.

div.head: CBEDF-Schedulable:
div.p: An instance I is CBEDF-schedulable if all behaviors of I can be scheduled correctly by CBEDF.

div.head: CBEDF Dominates OCBP
div.p: Recent works in [5,11,10] proposed Own Criticality Based Priority (OCBP) scheduling algorithm for certifiable mixed-criticality systems on a preemptive uniprocessor platform. In this section, we will show that CBEDF scheduling algorithm dominates OCBP scheduling algorithm.

Lemma 1 There is an instance I which is not OCBP-schedulable, but CBEDF-schedulable on a unit-speed processor. To schedule the instance in Example 3, OCBP scheduling algorithm requires a 1.25 speed-up processor [3]. It means that the instance is not OCBP-schedulable on a unit-speed processor. On the other hand, all the behaviors of the instance can be scheduled by CBEDF scheduling algorithm on a unit-speed processor.

Suppose we apply CBEDF scheduling algorithm to the above instance. Then, J3 is dispatched first as shown in the first figure of Figure 6. At time 1, there are two possible cases. First case is that the dispatched job J3 is not finished by its C3(LO) units of time. Then, L(I) becomes HI. Thus, behavior (1, 1, 2, 2) and (1, 1, 2, 1) can be scheduled correctly as shown in the second and third figure of Figure 6, respectively. Second case is that the dispatched job J3 is finished by its C3(LO) units of time. Then, 1 unit of re-maining slack is formed, which is allocated to a LO critical job J1. At time 2, J4 is dispatched. At time 3, there are two possible cases as at time 1. If J4 cannot finish using C4(LO) units of time for its execution, then behavior (1, 1, 1, 2) can be scheduled correctly as shown in the fourth figure of Figure 6. Otherwise, behavior (1, 1, 1, 1) can be scheduled correctly as shown in the last figure of Figure 6 . Hence, the above instance is CBEDF-schedulable.
Lemma 2 If an instance I is OCBP-schedulable, then the instance I is CBEDF-schedulable on a unit-speed processor.

Proof: OCBP scheduling algorithm can generate multiple scheduling orders for an OCBP-schedulable instance. We can prove Lemma 2 by showing that there is at least one priority set(scheduling order) which has EDF order for jobs having same criticality.

According to [5,11], OCBP-scheduling algorithm determines priority of jobs by selecting the lowest priority job repetitively. The repetition is done by excluding the selected lowest priority job. Candidates for the lowest priority job have the following property: Property: Candidates for the lowest priority job Ji are guaranteed at least Ci(χi) units of time between its release time and its deadline if every higher priority jobs Jj execute using Cj(χi) units of time. Thus, we can define the candidates formally as follows:

div.p: Observation 1 Suppose we select the latest deadline job in I candidate as the lowest priority job. Then, non-candidate job J k cannot have later deadline than the selected lowest priority job's deadline Di when χ k = χi.

Proof: Because Ji is the selected lowest priority job, inequality (1) is satisfied. Since J k is not a candidate job, J k cannot meet its deadline if every higher priority job Jj executes using Cj(χ k ) units of time. Hence, inequality (2) is satisfied.

Suppose J k has later deadline than Ji when χ k = χi. Then, inequality (3) is satisfied. However, inequalities (1), ( 2) and (3) contradict. Hence, J k cannot have later deadline than Ji when χ k = χi.

From these reasons, if an instance I is OCBP-schedulable, then the instance I is CBEDF-schedulable on a unit-speed processor.

div.head: LOAD-BASED SCHEDULABILITY ANAL-YSIS
div.p: As stated in the previous section, CBEDF scheduling algorithm dominates OCBP scheduling algorithm. It means that the number of CBEDF-schedulable instances is larger than that of OCBP-schedulable instances. In this section, we analyze what instances can be scheduled by CBEDF.

According to [11], an instance I is OCBP-schedulable, if I satisfies a condition Load 2 LO (I) + LoadHI(I) ≤ 1. To see what instances can be scheduled by CBEDF, we need to find a condition like OCBP's one above.

If an instance I is CBEDF-schedulable, I is correctly scheduled by CBEDF regardless of its runtime behavior. In other words, Ci(HI) units of time should be guaranteed for Proof: before proving the above theorem, we first define LoadMIX(I) which is the same as LoadLO(Itrans). Itrans will be explained later.
Load MIX (I) = max

div.p: ,where D i = Di -Ci(HI) + Ci(LO), t1 is the release time of a job and t3 is D i of a job. Thus, we need n 2 time to calculate LoadMIX(I) to consider all the time intervals [t1, t3]. We prove Theorem 2 by showing that the two conditions LoadMIX(I) ≤ 1 and LoadHI(I) ≤ 1 guarantee schedulability of LO and HI criticality levels, respectively.
Case 1) Criticality level of a behavior is HI.

If L(I) is HI, all HI critical jobs should be guaranteed to reserve their Ci(HI) units of time between their release times and deadlines. As we explained above, CBEDF scheduling algorithm preferentially allocates Ci(HI) units of time to all HI critical jobs, after which remaining slacks and empty slacks are used by LO critical jobs. Thus, all HI critical jobs are obviously guaranteed to reserve Ci(HI) units of time between their release times and their deadlines if LoadHI(I) ≤ 1 because Load(I) ≤ 1 is a sufficient schedulability condition for EDF scheduling algorithm [13] (p180).

div.p: If L(I) is LO, all jobs should be guaranteed to reserve their Ci(LO) units of time. Since all HI critical jobs are preferentially allocated Ci(HI) units of time, LoadLO(I) ≤ 1 cannot guarantee schedulability of the instance when L(I) is LO. The reason is illustrated with Example 4 below.

div.head: EVALUATION
div.p: In this section, we will present simulation results to evaluate the performance of the proposed CBEDF schedulability test.

div.head: Evaluation Setting
div.p: We evaluated the proposed CBEDF schedulability test with randomly generated instance sets. To generate jobs of an instance, we used the random function "rand()"in the GCC library. We generated jobs of an instance with keeping properties described in Table 1. As shown in Table 1, we limit the maximum time of an instance by 10000 and maximum execution time of a job by 200. It means that any job cannot be created or executed after 10000 units of time and any job cannot executes more than 200 units of time. All the generated jobs satisfy the following condition:
div.formula: 0 ≤ Ai ≤ Ai + Ci(LO) ≤ Ai + Ci(HI) ≤ Di ≤ 10000
div.p: To determine the maximum number of jobs in an instance, we calculate the average of LoadLO(I) with a randomly generated instance set. The results are shown in Figure 9.

Average of LoadLO(I) becomes larger than 1 if the number of jobs of an instance becomes larger than 70. Because instances cannot be scheduled without deadline miss if LoadLO(I) > 1, approximately, experiments with more than 100 jobs are meaningless. Thus, we experimented with the instances which have 10, 20, 30,...,90, 100 jobs. For each number of jobs, we generated 20000 instances. Hence, we generated total 200000 instances for this experiment. div.head: Evaluation Results
div.p: Figure 10 shows the percentages of instances which are proven to be schedulable by four schedulability tests. Figure 10 (a) shows that CBEDF significantly outperforms EDF and OCBP regardless of the number of jobs in an instance. In the figure, instances which pass OCBP and EDF are rapidly decreased as the number of jobs in an instance is increased. The percentage reduces to 0% when the number of jobs in an instance is over 70. The Figure 10 (a) also shows that schedulability of CBEDF is very similar to that of Clairvoyant. The maximum difference of coverage is 1.5% and average difference is 0.8% between CBEDF and Clairvoyant. These results demonstrate that CBEDF have very powerful performance because Clairvoyant scheudling is optimal for certifiable dual-criticality systems. When we limit deadlines of jobs from 10000 to 'Ai + Ci(HI) + rand(2000)' to pose more limit on deadlines, our algorithm still outperforms EDF and OCBP as shown in the Figure 10 (b). From the results, we see that most mixed-criticality schedulable instances (including Clairvoyant-schedulable instance) can be scheduled by our scheduling algorithm. Although we do not show that CBEDF is optimal in this paper, we show that CBEDF scheduling algorithm have similar performance to that of Clairvoyant scheduling algorithm.

div.head: CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
div.p: Mixed-criticality systems require certifications by multiple certification agencies. This demands efficient scheduling algorithms and schedulability tests that can handle as many job instances as possible with different levels of criticality. For this purpose, we proposed an EDF-based new dynamic scheduling algorithm called CBEDF for certifiable mixedcriticality systems. CBEDF consists of two sub-algorithms: offline empty slack location discovery algorithm and job scheduling algorithm at runtime. We show that CBEDF dominates previously proposed scheduling algorithms (EDF, OC-BP) [2,3,4]. In addition, we proposed a load-based sufficient schedulability test for CBEDF. We show that our proposed test for CBEDF outperforms other schedulability tests [3] by performing experiments using randomly generated instance sets. Although, it is not easy to extend proposed work in this paper to more general systems such as multicriticality and sporadic task system, we are challenging to extend it.

figure.figDesc: Figure 8: Each behavior of an instance can be split into either HI or LO, not both all HI critical jobs when L(I) is HI. And, Ci(LO) units of time should be guaranteed for all jobs when L(I) is LO. Since each behavior of an instance cannot belong to both HI and LO criticality levels, the two criticality levels are independent of each other as shown in Figure 8. Thus, an instance I can be certified by analyzing schedulability for each criticality level, separately. Suppose that one condition (A) guarantees CBEDF schedulabilty of a given instance, I, when L(I) is LO. And then, the other condition (B) guarantees CBEDF schedulability of I when L(I) is HI. If I satisfies both the conditions A and B, then the instance can be scheduled by CBEDF. Theorem 2 (CBEDF Schedulability) If an instance I satisfies two conditions LoadMIX(I) ≤ 1 and LoadHI(I) ≤ 1, then I is CBEDF schedulable.

div.p: Example 4 Consider an instance I comprised of four jobs. The jobs are characterized as below. J1 = (0, 5, LO, {2, 2}, 0) J2 = (0, 8, LO, {1, 1}, 0) J3 = (0, 6, HI, {3, 4}, 0) J4 = (0, 2, HI, {1, 1}, 1)

Suppose the behavior of I is (2, 1, 3, 1), then the criticality level of the behavior is LO. If we have a knowledge of runtime behavior of the instance before execution, then we can schedule the instance in (J4, J1, J3, J2) order. However, unfortunately, having the knowledge of runtime behavior before the execution is impossible.

Thus, it is hard to know whether HI critical jobs will execute longer than Ci(LO) units of time or not before execution. Hence, Ci(LO) units of time should be finished at least by Di -Ci(HI) + Ci(LO) units of time to guarantee deadline hit of Ji. By this reason, 3 units of time should be executed for J3 by unit time 5 in Example 4. It means that, 6 units (2 units for J1, 3 units for J3, 1 units for J4) of time are required in interval [0, 5]. However, it is impossible. Consequently, there is no correct scheduling order for the instance although LoadLO(I) ≤ 1. (LoadLO(I) is maximum value among four interval cases; [0,2]=0.5, [0,5]=0.6, [0,6]=1, [0,8]=0.875).

As shown in the above example, LoadLO(I) ≤ 1 cannot guarantee schedulability of an instance when L(I) is LO. If we can virtually transform HI critical jobs to LO critical jobs when we certify LO criticality level without any impacts on certification of HI criticality level, then LoadLO(I) ≤ 1 can be used to certify LO criticality level because all jobs have same criticality from the transformation.

It is possible to transform HI critical jobs to LO critical jobs virtually by subtracting Ci(HI) -Ci(LO) units of time from HI critical job's deadline without any impacts on certification of HI criticality level by the following reason.

Reason: Even though a HI critical job Ji is executes longer than Ci(LO) units of time at runtime, it does not affect the schedulability of HI criticality behaviors because the job can finish always before its deadline if Ci(LO) units of time can be finished by Di -Ci(HI) + Ci(LO).
